890.title: the mouth full of universe
890.carry: a little dirt on his lips
890.howItsDone: Krishna devotees tell this story alongside the butter-thief stories, and devotional paintings and songs show Yashoda peering into the child's open mouth.

segments.voice: Last week ended with the butter thief dragging a mortar between two trees, and two cursed brothers walking free. Your line was two trees fall, two men go free. What was within reach, right where you were stuck? Day eight hundred ninety.

Mother, Krishna ate dirt! The other boys come running to tell on him, his older brother Balarama among them. Small children put things in their mouths, and this one has just put a handful of earth in his. Yashoda grabs him by the hand, scolds him, and asks why. And the little boy, standing there with dirt on his lips, looks his mother in the eye and denies everything. Today, a toddler's lie, and a very strange answer to it.

His defense is simple. I didn't eat any dirt, Mother. They're lying. If you think they're telling the truth, look in my mouth yourself. So he opens it, and she looks in. And there, inside her son's mouth, she sees everything. The Bhagavata lists it, as if it can hardly stop: the sky and the directions, the mountains, the islands and the oceans, the whole round earth, the wind and fire, the moon and the stars. The turning of time. The gods. The elements that make up a body, and the mind itself. And then, in among all of it, she sees the village of Vraja. And in the village, she sees herself. Where does that put her? She's standing in her yard looking into her son's mouth, and inside his mouth she finds her yard, and herself standing in it. The text doesn't let her off easily. She's frightened. She asks: is this a dream? Is this some illusion sent by God? Is my own mind confused? Or is it some power that belongs to my child? She doesn't know what to call it. So she does the only thing that seems to fit. She bows, inwardly, to the one who is beyond all thought, in whom all of this rests. Here is what the story is saying. The baby she nurses, the boy she ties to a mortar, the one who steals the neighbors' butter, holds everything that is. Not as a picture of it. All of it, her included. And the doorway to that vision is a small boy's open mouth, with a little dirt on his lips.

891.title: the mouth full of universe
891.howItsDone: In some Krishna traditions, devotees relate to Krishna as Yashoda and Nanda do, as a beloved child, caring for small images of the infant Krishna with food, clothing and lullabies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a little dirt on his lips: Yashoda looked for dirt and saw everything, her own village and herself inside it. What small thing turned out bigger than you expected? Day eight hundred ninety-one.

It wasn't the first time. A chapter earlier, the Bhagavata tells a smaller version. Yashoda is nursing her baby, and he yawns, the way babies do. And in that yawn, for an instant, she sees the sky, the earth, the stars, the oceans, mountains and forests. She trembles and shuts her eyes. Then the moment passes and he's just a yawning baby again. So yesterday's vision was not her first. And that raises the question for today: after you've seen something like that, what happens to the next ordinary morning?
screen: `A YAWN WHILE NURSING.` → `SKY, EARTH, STARS, FOR AN INSTANT.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?`

segments.voice: Back in the yard, Yashoda is still standing over her son, bewildered, bowing inwardly to whatever this is. And then the text says something startling. Krishna spreads his maya over her, his power to veil, and it takes the form of a mother's love for her son. And she forgets. The vision is gone. She picks him up, sets him on her lap, and her heart is full of affection for him, just as it was before. The very next thing we hear is that she's his mother again, as if nothing happened. Notice what the story chooses. It could have ended with Yashoda as a great sage, transformed forever, seeing God in her child every waking moment. Instead the vision is taken back, on purpose, and what replaces it is love. The Bhagavata treats that love as no small thing. King Parikshit, listening to the story, asks the sage telling it: what did Nanda and Yashoda ever do, to be given a love like this? And the sage answers with a story about a former life, in which they asked for one thing: supreme devotion to the Lord, once they were born on earth. In this telling, being his parents is how that wish is granted. So the forgetting isn't a loss in this telling. It's the gift working. Some devotional schools hold up Yashoda's love, a parent's love, as a very sweet way of loving God: not bowing to the infinite from far away, but feeding him, scolding him, holding him. She has seen what he is. And she is allowed to keep loving who he is to her.

892.title: Kaliya
892.howItsDone: Pilgrims in Vrindavan visit a bathing place on the Yamuna associated with Kaliya, and some festivals reenact the boy Krishna's leap into the river.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maya, the forgetting is the gift: Yashoda saw everything, then was given back her ordinary love. Did you simply enjoy someone familiar? Day eight hundred ninety-two.

A hot day by the Yamuna. The boy Krishna is old enough now to take the calves and cows out to graze with his friends. It's summer, and on this day Balarama isn't with them. The boys and the cattle, desperate with thirst, come down to a part of the river and drink. And they drop where they stand, cowherds and cows alike, lifeless at the water's edge. Krishna sees them. He looks at them, the text says, with a glance full of nectar, and they get up, puzzled, as if waking from sleep. Something is wrong with that water.
screen: `A HOT DAY BY THE YAMUNA.` → `THEY DRINK, AND FALL.` → `A GLANCE BRINGS THEM BACK.`

segments.voice: What's wrong with the water is Kaliya. In a deep pool of the Yamuna lives a great serpent, a naga with many hoods, and his poison has turned the pool into something boiling and deadly. The Bhagavata says birds flying over it fall out of the sky. The plants on its banks are dead. Krishna decides the river has to be made clean again. On the bank stands a tall kadamba tree. He climbs it, tightens his clothes, slaps his arms like a wrestler, and jumps, right into the poisoned pool. The water heaves. Kaliya rises, furious that someone has entered his home. He sees a small, dark, beautiful boy playing in the water, and he bites him, and wraps him in his coils. And Krishna goes still. Up in the village, the people see terrible omens, and they look for Krishna, and he isn't there. The whole village runs to the river: the women, the old men, the children, the cows. They follow his footprints to the bank and see him there, motionless, wrapped in a serpent. Yashoda wants to go into the water after him. Nanda does too. The gopis cling to her, grieving. And one person on that bank is calm. Balarama, the text says, knows his brother's power, and he holds them back, and smiles. So the chapter leaves us in a strange place. A whole village in despair on the riverbank. One brother quietly smiling. And in the water, the boy they love, perfectly still, inside the coils.

893.title: Kaliya
893.howItsDone: Krishna dancing on Kaliya's hoods, Kaliya-mardana, appears in temple sculpture, bronzes, paintings and classical dance, and devotees tell it among the stories of Krishna's childhood in Vraja.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kaliya: the boy went still in the serpent's coils, the village wept on the bank, and Balarama smiled. Where did you take one calm breath before reacting? Day eight hundred ninety-three.

Why does he go still? In the Bhagavata's telling, he isn't overpowered. It describes him lying in the coils for a while, and then it turns the camera to the bank, to his mother and friends and the cows, all of them stricken. Then it turns back to the water. Krishna sees them. He sees what his stillness is doing to the people who love him, and the text says he stays bound, playing the part of a mortal, only for a short time. Then he decides that's enough. Today, the boy gets up.
screen: `WHY DOES HE GO STILL?` → `HE SEES THE GRIEF ON THE BANK.` → `THAT'S ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Krishna makes his body grow. The coils, which were holding a small boy, are suddenly stretched around something they can't contain, and Kaliya has to let go. The serpent rears up, hissing, his eyes burning, his breath smoking with poison, and the two of them circle in the water, Krishna moving around him the way Garuda, the great eagle, circles a snake. Kaliya follows him until he's worn out. And then Krishna does something stranger. He presses down Kaliya's raised hoods, climbs up onto them, and begins to dance. The text treats it as a real performance. Celestial musicians gather. Drums and songs and flowers come down from the sky. And on the stage of the serpent's heads, the boy dances. Whichever hood Kaliya lifts, Krishna's feet come down on it, keeping time. Kaliya thrashes and then weakens. Blood comes from his mouths. His hoods are broken, his pride with them. And at last, exhausted, the serpent turns his mind toward the one dancing on him, and, the text says, remembers the ancient Lord. What Krishna leaves undone matters. He doesn't kill Kaliya. He doesn't strike him with a weapon. The fight becomes a dance, and the dance goes on until the poison in the serpent's pride is gone. In Hindu art and song the scene is known as Kaliya-mardana, the subduing of Kaliya: a small boy, one foot raised, dancing on a cobra's hood.

894.title: Kaliya
894.carry: spared, and sent to the ocean
894.howItsDone: Devotees retell the prayer of Kaliya's wives as a model of surrender, and in some depictions of Kaliya-mardana the naga wives are shown with joined palms beside the serpent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kaliya: the boy danced on the serpent's hoods until his pride was gone, and the serpent remembered the Lord. Did you meet an old habit with rhythm instead of a fight? Day eight hundred ninety-four.

The serpent is beaten. He lies broken in the water, and the boy is still standing on his heads. And now, out of the pool, come the serpent's wives. The Bhagavata calls them the naga wives, and they don't come to fight. They come with their children in front of them, their hair loose, their clothes disordered, and they bow down before Krishna with their palms joined. Kaliya can't speak for himself anymore. So they speak for him. Today belongs to the wives, and to what happens after a battle is won.
screen: `THE SERPENT IS BEATEN.` → `HIS WIVES COME OUT OF THE POOL.` → `THEY SPEAK FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: What the wives say is surprising. They don't argue that their husband is innocent. They say his punishment is fair. More than fair: they call it a grace. Your feet have touched his head, they say, and others perform long austerities hoping for the dust of those feet. Then they ask for one thing: spare him. He is our husband. Let him live. And Krishna lets him go. Kaliya, slowly, gets his breath back, and he speaks plainly. We serpents are born this way, he says. Angry by nature, with poison in us. It's hard to let go of what you're made of. Krishna doesn't lecture him. He gives him a way forward. Leave this pool, he says. Go to the ocean with your family, so the river can be clean again for the people and the cows. Then Krishna names the fear that brought Kaliya here in the first place. He was hiding. Garuda, the eagle who preys on serpents, could not enter this pool, because of a sage's old curse. So this poisoned corner of the Yamuna was the one place he felt safe. And Krishna answers that fear. Garuda won't harm you now, he says, because you carry the marks of my feet on your hoods. So the story ends without anyone destroyed. The poison leaves the river. The serpent leaves with his family, his fear answered. And the very feet that broke his pride become the thing that protects him.
screen: `"YOUR FEET HAVE TOUCHED HIS HEAD."` · `"WE ARE BORN THIS WAY."` · `GO TO THE OCEAN; LET THE RIVER BE CLEAN.` · then, large: `THE FOOTPRINTS PROTECT HIM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind someone you struggle with, someone whose sharpness you've felt. Now, gently, wonder about one thing: what might they be afraid of? What corner did they crawl into to feel safe? You don't have to excuse anything. Just let that one question soften the picture a little as you breathe. Then, if you can, wish them somewhere better to live than their poison. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Kaliya. The serpent spared at his wives' plea, sent to the ocean, and protected by the very footprints that subdued him.
Your line: spared, and sent to the ocean. Today, when someone is sharp with you, ask quietly what they might be hiding from. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

895.title: Govardhan lifted
895.howItsDone: Some Hindu communities keep Govardhan Puja, in the days of Diwali, by building a small hill of food, called Annakut, and offering it, and pilgrims walk around Govardhan hill near Vrindavan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kaliya was spared: sent to the ocean, protected by the footprints on his hoods. When someone was sharp with you, did you wonder what they were hiding from? Day eight hundred ninety-five.

The whole village is cooking. Pots of rice, sweets, milk dishes, everything the cowherds can make. The elders are busy getting ready for a sacrifice. Krishna, a boy now, watches all this, and he already knows the answer, the text says, but he goes to his father anyway and asks. Father, what's all this for? Who is it for? What do we get from it? Nanda is patient with him. It's for Indra, he says, the king of the gods, the lord of the rain clouds. Today a boy questions a custom, and a whole village changes what it does.
screen: `THE WHOLE VILLAGE IS COOKING.` → `"FATHER, WHAT'S THIS FOR?"` → `"FOR INDRA, LORD OF RAIN."`

segments.voice: Nanda explains. Indra sends the rain. The rain grows the grass. The grass feeds the cows, and the cows feed us. So we honor him with this sacrifice. Krishna answers with a different picture of the world. Beings are born and die by their own actions, he says. Happiness and trouble come from what we do. And what do we, cowherds, actually live by? Not cities, not kingdoms. We live in forests and on hills. Our wealth is the cows. So let's offer to what is right in front of us: to the cows, to the brahmins, and to the hill, Govardhan, which shelters us and our herds. And he gives detailed instructions. Cook all the food you were going to cook. Feed the brahmins. Feed everyone, even the dogs, even the people at the edges of the village. Give the cows fresh grass. Dress well, decorate the cattle, and walk around the hill. Nanda and the elders listen, and they agree. They do every bit of it. Then the text adds a strange and lovely detail. As the people offer their food to the hill, Krishna takes on a vast new form, and declares, I am the hill. And that great form eats the offerings. At the same time, the boy Krishna is standing among the cowherds, bowing to it with them. The god of the hill and the boy worshiping the hill are one person. The cowherds walk around Govardhan, singing. It feels like a festival. Somewhere up in the sky, Indra has noticed what's missing.

896.title: Govardhan lifted
896.howItsDone: Krishna as Giridhari, the one who holds up the hill, is a familiar name and image in Hindu devotion, and on Govardhan Puja some communities build a small hill of food and offer it in memory of this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Govardhan lifted began with a question: the village turned its offering from Indra to the hill, the cows and the brahmins. What near thing did you thank? Day eight hundred ninety-six.

Indra is furious. The king of the gods has been passed over by a village of cowherds, on the advice of a child. So he calls up the clouds that are kept, the text says, for the end of the world, and sends them over Vraja. The sky goes black. Rain comes down in torrents, with hail, lightning and a wind that knocks over everything standing. The fields flood. The cows shiver, and shield their calves with their bodies. The cowherds, soaked and terrified, gather around the boy who started all this. Krishna, protect us.
screen: `INDRA IS FURIOUS.` → `THE CLOUDS OF THE WORLD'S END.` → `"KRISHNA, PROTECT US."`

segments.voice: Krishna looks at the storm and understands it. This is Indra's pride, he thinks, and the people who depend on me are in danger because of it. So he walks to the hill, Govardhan, and lifts it. With one hand. The Bhagavata's picture is wonderfully small: he holds it up as easily as a child holds up a mushroom. Then he calls out to everyone: come under. Bring your cows, your carts, your families, everything. Don't be afraid it will fall. And the whole village comes in under the hill, out of the rain, into the dry. He holds it up for seven days, the text says, without moving from the spot, not hungry, not thirsty, while the cowherds look up at him. Outside, Indra pours down everything he has. Under the hill, nothing reaches them. At last Indra is astonished, and his pride gives way. He calls the clouds back. The sky clears, the sun comes out, and Krishna tells everyone to go home, and sets the hill back exactly where it was. The village crowds around him, embracing him, his mother among them. Now look back at this week. A mother looks into a mouth and sees everything, and is given the grace to forget. A serpent is subdued with a dance and sent away safe. A village asks why, and turns to the hill that shelters it. And then that hill becomes a roof. The hill they fed holds off the storm when the sky falls.
